title: FOAM: Frequency and Operator-Error Based Adaptive Damping Method for Reducing Staleness-Oriented Error for Shampoo
claim: Our adaptive method reaches better loss and accuracy than the stale-update baseline in less wall-clock time across tasks and hyperparameters.
layout: 4 scatter panels in a row; shaded blue win-region bounded by dashed baseline lines
description: Four side-by-side scatter plots show wall-clock time in minutes on the x-axis against a quality metric on the y-axis. Panels (a) and (b) are ViT on ImageNet, showing train loss and validation accuracy. Panels (c) and (d) are Conformer on LibriSpeech, showing train loss and validation WER. The stale-update Shampoo baselines are red circles and triangles. Many blue hollow markers of different shapes are FOAM hyperparameter settings. Dashed horizontal and vertical lines pass through the baseline points. They mark a light-blue shaded rectangle for the region that is both faster and better. Most blue markers fall inside it. Grey legend boxes list the settings. Panel captions sit below each plot.
caption: Wall-clock efficiency comparison between Shampoo with stale update and \alg update. Figure [ref]-[ref] presents the best training loss and validation accuracy for the ViT (ImageNet-1K) task, while Figure [ref]-[ref] shows the training loss and WER for the Conformer (LibriSpeech) task. In all plots, the blue rectangular areas represent the region of superior performance, where \alg achieves better convergence and final metrics in significantly less wall-clock time than the stale-update baselines.
abstract: Shampoo is attracting considerable attention for its superior performance on large-scale optimization benchmarks; yet it faces a significant practical bottleneck: the prohibitive computational overhead of matrix inversion. To mitigate this, practitioners typically rely on stale preconditioner updates, creating a fundamental trade-off between computational efficiency and optimization fidelity. In this work, we provide a theoretical study of staleness through the complementary lenses of convergence and stability. While staleness improves computational efficiency, it inherently degrades performance and introduces numerical instability. Crucially, we identify that damping, acting as a numerical stabilizer, can effectively suppress these negative effects. Guided by this analysis, we propose FOAM, an adaptive algorithm that stabilizes training by dynamically controlling both the damping factor and the eigendecomposition frequency based on an approximation of the staleness-oriented error. Experimental results demonstrate that FOAM reduces wall-clock time compared to standard Shampoo while maintaining robust convergence.
